item.title: How Small Can a Single Shor Run Be? Limits and Constructions for secp256k1
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Splitting and symmetry-exploiting windowed circuits shrink the largest quantum run for breaking secp256k1 by a factor of 3.87 to volume B=0.2585B0 (1,246 logical qubits, 11.87×106 Toffoli gates) at a total volume T=8.79T0. A linear Shor run superposing exponent set S reveals at most log2⁡(1+(|S|−1)/r) bits about a uniform key of group order r, limiting splitting alone to a 1.86-fold reduction.

Grade 0.426 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Yicheng Guang, Yuliang Xiong, Yueqi Chen, Xun Gao

Figure

Largest-run volume B/B0 plotted against total volume T/T0. It highlights the theoretical floor for splitting alone under baseline arithmetic alongside points achieved by Ekerå's tradeoff and the paper's optimized window configurations.

Asks

How small can the spacetime volume of the largest quantum run in Shor's algorithm for secp256k1 be made when splitting the computation across multiple runs within fixed total-volume and classical-processing budgets?

Before

Baseline single-run design of Häner et al. had volume B0=5.72×1010 (1,457 qubits, 39.3×106 Toffoli gates); Ekerå's tradeoff on the ECDSA.Fail addition core reached a 2.81-fold reduction at T=7.71T0.

But

Budgets capped at total volume T≤10T0 relative to three runs of Häner et al. (T0=3B0), ≤240 classical operations, and key recovery success probability ≥0.99. Evaluated via 563 classical Monte Carlo trials per configuration.

Tools

unit-orbit and mixed-radix point-addition windows · ECDSA.Fail leaderboard point-addition core · semiclassical QFT · lattice decoder · randomized-scalar and randomized-start circuit certification

Abstract

Most resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with Shor's algorithm describe one long run per attempt, and the spacetime volume of that run, its peak number of logical qubits times its Toffoli count, sets its logical-error budget. Ekerå's tradeoff shrinks each run by using more runs, but how far it can shrink the largest run, and at what circuit cost, has not been determined. We minimize the volume of the largest run while every key is recovered with probability at least 0.99, within ten times the total volume of three runs of Häner et al. and 2⁴⁰ classical operations. We prove that a linear run fixed in advance, which starts its group register at a point and discards its label, reveals at most log₂(1+(|S|-1)/r) bits about a uniform key, where |S| counts its exponent values and r is the group order. With generic post-processing and the baseline's window costs, splitting alone then shrinks the largest run at most 1.86 times within the budget. To gain more, we make each exponent bit cheaper with windows that share one table point among exponent values related by six symmetries of the curve, on a point-addition core borrowed from the ECDSA.Fail leaderboard. One random scalar and one random start per run give every approximate addition uniform operands, and a bound on each run's outcomes certifies, for every key, a decoder that discards flagged runs. We count every Toffoli gate and every qubit of every run, and each configuration solved all 563 of its pre-registered simulated trials on secp256k1. The best one shrinks the largest run 3.87 times at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume, against 2.81 times for Ekerå's tradeoff on the same core, and its run is at least 2.6 times smaller than every design of Initio Intelligence.

item.title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Defines strategic milestones for DOE fault-tolerant quantum computing: target deployment in 2028 with at least 100 logical qubits and 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations, scaling into the 2030s to 1,000–10,000 logical qubits and 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations.

Grade 0.419 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright

Asks

What strategy, milestones, and infrastructure must the US Department of Energy develop to deploy fault-tolerant quantum computers for scientific utility by 2028 and scale into the 2030s?

But

Contingent on ongoing advances in commercial hardware roadmaps and demonstration of scaled logical operations on error-corrected qubits.

Tools

fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) roadmap · systems software and facility integration analysis · logical qubit architectures

Abstract

Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

item.title: Validity and maximum violation of the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound for linear stabilizer codes
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Linear entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes [[n,k,d;c]]_q obey the Brun–Devetak–Hsieh (BDH) bound 2(d−1)≤n−k+c whenever the number of logical qudits exceeds the Singleton defect (k>σ=n−k−d+1), even if degenerate. When k=σ, the bound overestimates entanglement by at most Mq(2k)−2k, a limit achieved by codes on normal rational curves.

Grade 0.416 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes” · Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim

Figure

Pairs c versus length n at q=8,k=2, illustrating the gap between the BDH bound, the Grassl–Huber–Winter bound, and the realized maximum violation Δ=5=M8(4)−4.

Asks

For which parameters is the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound valid, and by how much can it overestimate required entanglement?

Before

Grassl, Huber and Winter (2022) established a generalized Singleton bound for large distances (d−1>n/2), but validity boundaries and maximum violations of the BDH bound for degenerate codes remained unknown.

But

Applies strictly to 𝔽q-linear stabilizer codes; non-additive codes and certain non-linear additive codes are excluded. Full maximum-violation equality at k=σ depends on known cases of the classical MDS conjecture.

Tools

Erasure and dimension-counting on qudit restrictions · Classical MDS code hulls and projective geometry · CaDiCaL SAT solver with DRAT refutation proofs · Lean 4 proof assistant

Abstract

Entanglement-assisted quantum codes protect quantum information with entangled pairs shared in advance, and the entanglement-assisted quantum Singleton bound of Brun, Devetak and Hsieh is the standard estimate of how many pairs they consume. Codes that violate it at large distance are known. For linear entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes, which include all qubit stabilizer codes of this kind, we determine when the bound holds and how far it can fail. The answer depends on how many qudits, together with the receiver's halves of the pairs, recover the logical qudits. If this number is less than twice the number of logical qudits, the bound holds, also for degenerate codes. If it is exactly twice that, the bound overstates the number of pairs by at most the length of the longest classical maximum distance separable (MDS) code of that dimension, minus the dimension. Codes carrying values and derivatives of polynomials on the projective line attain this maximum whenever the field size is at least that dimension and the MDS conjecture is known for it, which includes every prime and, by a recently announced result, every even field size. If the number is more than twice the number of logical qudits, the violation is bounded in terms of the lengths of classical codes of a given Singleton defect, and the bound is attained for one logical qudit. Apart from cited MDS lengths, the proofs are formalized in the Lean proof assistant.

item.title: Schur saturation and the Clifford ceiling in qudit CSS codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — CSS self-orthogonality enforces dual Schur saturation C(A)⟂∗C(A)⟂=𝔽pG, confining all strictly CSS-preserving local-diagonal transversal gates to Clifford hierarchy level ≤2. Even when ℓ-orthogonality holds up to ℓ=p−2, the degree ≥3 non-Clifford sector vanishes completely.

Grade 0.408 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · José Alberto Guzmán-Vega, Juan Carlos Jiménez-Cervantes, Eliseo Sarmiento-Rosales

Asks

Can a CSS code family satisfy orthogonality-type certificates to arbitrarily high order while admitting no transversal non-Clifford gate?

But

Restricted to strictly CSS-preserving local-diagonal gates expressed as sums of single-site phases in the computational basis for prime p≥5. Does not constrain non-diagonal transversal gates, basis changes, nonlocal diagonal phases, or ancilla-assisted protocols.

Tools

Schur product saturation · character evaluation codes on finite abelian groups · polarization of local polynomial phases · Cui–Gottesman–Krishna Clifford hierarchy classification

Code. https://github.com/JAGV-Math/SchurSaturation

Abstract

Orthogonality-type conditions (triorthogonality in the qubit setting and its prime-dimensional analogues), are the primary algebraic screening criterion for transversal non-Clifford gate constructions in CSS codes. In every known positive construction the certificate is accompanied by a non-Clifford logical gate, leaving open whether a CSS family can satisfy these conditions to arbitrarily high order while admitting no such gate. We answer this question for the class of symmetric spectral CSS codes Q(A)=CSS(C(A),C(A)) built from character evaluation on a finite abelian group G with exp(G)|p-1, p≥5 prime. The mechanism is the identity \[C(A)^⊥ * C(A)^⊥=F_p^G,\] which we call Schur saturation of the dual code. It follows from the CSS self-orthogonality condition A∩(-A)=varnothing and annihilates every local polynomial phase of degree ≥3. The complete gate-group classification S^CSS_(≤p-1)(A)=C(A)^⊥ ⊕C(Stab(A)) shows that every strictly CSS-preserving local-diagonal transversal gate lies at level ≤2 of the Clifford hierarchy, a structural bound we call the Clifford ceiling. The criterion extends to arbitrary CSS pairs satisfying C_Z^⊥ * C_Z^⊥=F_pⁿ; the LDPC instance [[58,16,3]]₅ is verified computationally. The false-positive character of the orthogonality certificates is sharpest in the Boolean toric family: these codes satisfy ℓ-orthogonality for ℓ≤p-2, yet the non-Clifford sector collapses to zero. The flagship instance [[64,56,3]]₅ encodes 56 logical ququints at rate R=0.875 with distance-3 protection, passes every orthogonality screening test, and yet admits no local-diagonal non-Clifford gate of any degree. The unique non-Pauli survivor is the uniform quadratic drive Q_u, fault-tolerant, logically nontrivial, and Clifford at level 2, carrying no magic-state resource.

item.title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — PP-VarQITE produces state-preparation circuits that are two to ten times shallower than sequential MPS compilations across frustrated chains and 2D lattices, running on Quantinuum Helios-1 up to 98 qubits at two-qubit depth at most 42.

Grade 0.400 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Cenk Tüysüz, Simon Deconihout, Enrico Rinaldi, Michele Grossi

Figure

Absolute thermal energy-density error versus native two-qubit gate count (left) and depth (right) for a 50-site frustrated chain (top) and a 7×7 TFIM (bottom), showing PP-VarQITE outperforming MPS compilation routes in circuit depth.

Asks

How can finite-temperature thermal states be prepared within shallow circuit depths on noisy quantum hardware using purely classical parameter determination?

Before

Sequential matrix-product-state compilation, which incurs an order-of-magnitude larger gate count and circuit depth to match accuracy.

But

Suffers from an imaginary-time variational delay at intermediate temperatures in frustrated and 2D systems; classical parameter generation requires truncating retained Pauli terms above coefficient threshold cmin⁡.

Tools

Pauli propagation · variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (VarQITE) · thermal purification · Quantinuum Helios-1 trapped-ion processor · Bell-frame recompilation

Abstract

Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a 7×7 Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. Through classical circuit design, we demonstrate low-temperature state preparation at circuit sizes beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.

item.arxave:abstract: Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a 7×7 Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. Through classical circuit design, we demonstrate low-temperature state preparation at circuit sizes beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.

item.title: Low-Degree Torus Approximations of the AND Function and ACC⁰ Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Torus polynomial degree approximating 𝖠𝖭𝖣n/2 is O(log⁡(n/ϵ)) for ϵ∈(0,1/4), matching the known lower bound. For depth-d, size-s 𝖠𝖢0[m] circuits, torus degree is at most Cmd(log⁡s)max⁡{1,μ−1}dlog⁡(1/ϵ) where μ is the number of distinct prime factors of m.

Grade 0.398 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Shuhei Osaki, Ryuhei Mori

Asks

What are the minimal degrees of torus polynomials needed to approximate the AND function and general 𝖠𝖢0[m] circuits over every input?

Before

Was O(log2⁡(n/ϵ)) for 𝖠𝖭𝖣n/2, and was (log⁡s)Om(d2)(log⁡(1/ϵ))Om(d) for 𝖠𝖢0[m] circuits (Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao 2019).

But

Worst-case input error (L∞ torus norm); ϵ∈(0,1/4); circuit gate types restricted to unbounded-fan-in 𝖠𝖭𝖣, 𝖬𝗈𝖽m, and 𝖭𝖮𝖳.

Tools

Fourier sampling · modular zero tests · finite-difference prime-power polynomial representations · circuit decomposition with alternating prime factors

Abstract

Torus polynomials, real polynomials evaluated modulo one, were proposed by Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao as a route to ACC⁰ lower bounds. We prove degree upper bounds for torus polynomials approximating a function on every input. First, for every ε∈(0,1/4), AND_n/2 has an ε-approximating torus polynomial of degree O(log(n/ε)), improving the previous O(log²(n/ε)). This is optimal up to constant factors for inverse-polynomial error, by a lower bound of Krishan and Vishwanathan, and refutes two superlogarithmic-degree conjectures of Krishan and Sarma. Second, for every Boolean function g computed by a depth-d, size-s AC⁰[m] circuit, g/2 has an ε-approximating torus polynomial of degree at most C_m^d(logs)^(max1,μ-1d)log(1/ε), where μ is the number of distinct prime factors of m and C_m depends only on m. This improves the bound (logs)^(O_m(d²))(log(1/ε))^(O_m(d)) of Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao, making the exponent of logs linear in the depth and the dependence on log(1/ε) linear. Both proofs sample terms of a Fourier expansion and approximate them by low-degree torus polynomials. A torus approximation of degree D can be written as a linear combination of at most (n+1)^D parities, called a periodic Fourier representation, which is known to give a non-adaptive measurement-based quantum computation with linear side-processing using one qubit per parity. Hence every ACC⁰ function can be computed with quasipolynomially many qubits and inverse-polynomial error probability on every input. Conversely, we prove that a periodic Fourier representation with r parities and error probability ε gives a torus approximation of degree O(log(r/ε)), so the two notions are equivalent.

item.title: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Two verifiable graph-state quantum advantage instances on IBM hardware are sampled classically on eight GPUs faster and with higher fidelity than hardware: exact ideal sampling for 70-qubit RGS70, and certified fidelity at least 0.908 for 64-qubit DCS64 with 314 T gates (versus 0.349 on hardware).

Grade 0.389 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Zhongpu Qiu, Yuqi Qing, Jielan Li, Hongxia Hao

Figure

Distribution of scaled output probabilities z=2np(x) for classical GPU samples and quantum hardware samples on RGS70 and DCS64 against ideal and noisy Porter-Thomas distributions.

Asks

Does the check structure required to verify quantum advantage in graph-state experiments fundamentally limit how classically hard the circuits can be?

Before

Hardware reported certified fidelity of at least 0.349 in 870 s for DCS64, and estimated classical sampling times up to 1025 s for RGS70.

But

Sampling cost depends on early axis rank and early Clifford entanglement rather than total T gate count; trade-off between checks and hardness holds conditionally once depth allows checks to cover the early region.

Tools

tensor-network contraction · rank-width methods for graph states · T-gate injection gadgetization · uniform-prefix sampling · 8-GPU cluster

Abstract

Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical ones on some tasks, but a convincing demonstration must be both hard to reproduce classically and verifiable. A recent proposal achieves verifiability by preparing graph states with built-in error detection, so that the quality of the experiment can be certified without simulating it; hardness is added by measuring in a non-Clifford basis or by inserting T gates. We show that the two instances posted to demonstrate this proposal on IBM hardware can be sampled classically on eight graphics processing units, with higher quality than the hardware in comparable or shorter time. For the 70-qubit instance our samples are drawn from the ideal output distribution; for the 64-qubit instance with 314 T gates they come with a certified fidelity of at least 0.908, against 0.349 for the hardware. The reason lies in verification itself: T gates can only be placed where the error detection cannot see them, which pushes them towards the end of the circuit, where they add little classical cost. Our results identify the features that future verifiable advantage experiments must control.

item.title: Spinal reflected entropy reveals logical magic
item.description:
Worth a look theory — The spinal reflected entropy between a disk A around the spine vertex and loop-aligned bands B decomposes as SR(n)(A:B)=αnL−4gγ+ζn(ψ), where the state-dependent logical term is exactly ζn(ψ)=Mn(ψ)+log⁡GSD.

Grade 0.385 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Zong-Yue Hou, Yuzhen Zhang, Zhi-Cheng Yang, Yingfei Gu

Figure

Planar fundamental domain of the torus partitioned into disk A and cycle bands B after puncturing disk D, and the doubled genus-2 surface Σ2 where bands sew into tubes carrying logical anyon charges.

Asks

Can an entanglement measure probe the noncommuting logical string operators simultaneously to directly quantify the magic of an encoded state in a topological stabilizer code?

Before

Topological entanglement entropy γ is constant across all code states, and entanglement cuts along single cycles probe string operators in only one commuting basis.

But

Pure logical states in ground-space manifolds of 2D qubit topological stabilizer codes. Does not hold for general stabilizer codes on ℤN qudits with composite N.

Tools

Reflected entropy / canonical Choi state purification · Spine retract partitioning · TQFT path-integral surgery · Bell sampling in tube-charge basis

Abstract

Entanglement and magic are usually regarded as independent quantum resources. Here we connect the two in the toric code, where the stabilizer Rényi entropy of the stored logical state, a widely used measure of magic, acquires a direct interpretation in terms of entanglement. We introduce the spinal reflected entropy, defined on a neighborhood of a spine of the underlying surface as the reflected entropy between a disk around the vertex of the spine and bands along its noncontractible loops. It obeys an area law with a topological correction and contains one additional term that carries all the dependence on the stored state. On a torus, this term equals the stabilizer Rényi entropy of the stored state plus the logarithm of the ground-state degeneracy. The mechanism is topological. On the surface sewn to its reflected copy, the bands close into tubes, logical Pauli operators become anyon charges threading them, and these charges are distributed as the outcomes of Bell sampling of the stored state. The result extends to surfaces of higher genus and to general two-dimensional topological stabilizer codes on qubits. Logical magic thus becomes a geometrically defined entanglement quantity, one that shallow circuits preserving the code space cannot change.
